summary: This Best Current Practice clarifies and updates requirements from RFCs 4787, 5382 and 5508 based on operational and development experience. It focuses on NAT from IPv4 to IPv4.

plainLanguage.summary: A NAT rewrites the addresses and ports of packets as they pass, and each rule about how it should do that leaves room for interpretation. This document closes the gaps that turned up in practice: how long a half-open connection is kept, what happens when a reset arrives, whether a mapping is shared between TCP and UDP, and when a mapping may be thrown away.

subtitle: The clarifications that make the NAT behavioural requirements usable in a real network.

tldr.problem: The three documents that define how a NAT must behave for UDP, TCP and ICMP left gaps that only show up once millions of devices are behind real translators, so two implementations could both be compliant and still behave differently.
tldr.mechanism: The document issues a series of updates and clarifications: a TCP state machine for session tracking, separate open and closing timeouts, rules for handling TCP resets, and defaults for mapping and filtering behaviour.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7857 is BCP 127 and updates RFC 4787, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508. It adds no new requirements beyond those documents and covers NAT44 only.

facts.label: Delay before deleting a reset session

today: RFC 7857 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 127, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. It updates RFC 4787, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508, and the requirements for Carrier-Grade NAT live separately in RFC 6888.

sections.title: Scope and Terminology
sections.content:
RFC 4787, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508 contributed to enhancing Network Address Translation interoperability and conformance. Operational experience gained through widespread deployment, and the evolution of NAT, indicates that some areas of the original documents need further clarification or updates, and this document provides such clarifications and updates.

The scope has been set so that the document does not create new requirements beyond those specified in the documents it updates. It focuses exclusively on NAT44, that is, translation from IPv4 to IPv4. Requirements related to Carrier-Grade NAT are defined in RFC 6888.

The reader is assumed to be familiar with the terminology defined in RFC 2663, RFC 4787, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508. In this document the term NAT refers to both Basic NAT and Network Address/Port Translator (NAPT). Basic NAT and NAPT are two variations of traditional NAT: translation in Basic NAT is limited to IP addresses alone, whereas translation in NAPT is extended to include IP addresses and transport identifiers such as a TCP or UDP port, or an ICMP query identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a patch, not a redesign. It only says what the existing NAT requirements meant, and it only covers the IPv4-to-IPv4 case, not the IPv6 flavours.

sections.title: TCP Session Tracking
sections.content:
RFC 5382 specifies TCP timers associated with various connection states but does not specify the TCP state machine a NAT44 should follow as a basis to apply such timers. The update is that the TCP state machine depicted in Figure 1, adapted from RFC 6146, should be implemented by a NAT for TCP session tracking purposes.

The machine starts in CLOSED. A client SYN moves the connection to INIT, and a server SYN moves it to ESTABLISHED. A data packet moves it from TRANS to ESTABLISHED, while a reset from the server or the client moves it back to TRANS. An established connection that goes idle past the established-connection timeout returns to TRANS, and the transitory-connection timeout returns it to CLOSED. A FIN from either side moves the connection to the corresponding FIN-received state, and the FIN from the other side moves it to the state where both FINs have been received, which is the state the transitory-connection timeout returns to CLOSED.
sections.plainLanguage: To time out a connection correctly you have to know which phase it is in, and the earlier document gave timers without giving the phases. This update supplies the phase machine: closed, opening, opening with data, established, and the two closing states.

sections.title: TCP Idle Timeouts and Resets
sections.content:
The transitory connection idle-timeout is the minimum time a TCP connection in the partially open or closing phases must remain idle before the NAT considers the associated session a candidate for removal. RFC 5382 does not clearly state whether the open and closing timeouts can be configured separately, and this document clarifies that a NAT should provide different configurable parameters for the open and closing idle timeouts.

To accommodate deployments that consider a partially open timeout of 4 minutes as excessive from a security standpoint, a NAT may allow the configured timeout to be less than 4 minutes. However, a minimum default transitory connection idle-timeout of 4 minutes is recommended.

RFC 5382 leaves the handling of TCP RST packets unspecified. The update adopts a similar default behaviour to RFC 6146: when the NAT receives a TCP RST matching an existing mapping, it must translate the packet according to the NAT mapping entry, and it should wait for 4 minutes before deleting the session and removing any state associated with it if no packets are received during that timeout. The NAT has to verify whether received RST packets belong to a connection, in order to avoid off-path attacks. And if the NAT immediately removes the mapping upon receipt of an RST, stale connections may be maintained by endpoints if the first RST is lost between the NAT and the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Two timers, and one reset rule. A half-open connection should be held for at least four minutes by default, and the two phases, opening and closing, should be timed separately. A reset packet ends a session, but not instantly: the translator keeps the state for four minutes in case the reset was lost.

sections.title: Port Overlapping and Address Pooling
sections.content:
REQ-1 from RFC 4787 and REQ-1 from RFC 5382 specify a port overlapping behaviour: the external IP address and port can be reused for connections originating from the same internal source IP address and port irrespective of the destination. This is known as Endpoint-Independent Mapping (EIM). This document clarifies that the behaviour may be extended to connections originating from different internal source IP addresses and ports as long as their destinations are different.

A NAT may implement the following mechanism: if destination addresses and ports are different for outgoing connections started by local clients, the NAT may assign the same external port as the source ports for the connections. The port overlapping mechanism manages mappings between external and internal packets by looking at and storing their 5-tuple: protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port. This enables concurrent use of a single NAT external port for multiple transport sessions, which allows a NAT to successfully process packets in a network that has a limited number of IP addresses.

The address pooling behaviour of Paired (APP) was recommended in REQ-2 from RFC 4787, but the behaviour when an external IPv4 address runs out of ports was left undefined. This document clarifies that if APP is enabled, new sessions from a host that already has a mapping associated with an external IP that ran out of ports should be dropped. A configuration parameter may be provided to allow a NAT to start using ports from another external IP address when the one that anchored the APP mapping ran out of ports. Tweaking this parameter is a trade-off between service continuity and strict APP enforcement, and this behaviour is sometimes called soft-APP. The recommendation for the particular case of a CGN is that an implementation must use the same external IP address mapping for all sessions associated with the same internal IP address, be they TCP, UDP, ICMP, something else, or a mix of different protocols. This behaviour should apply also for TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: One address and one port can carry several connections, as long as the destinations differ, because the translator keeps the whole five-part description of each flow. The other half is about pairing: when a host's address is pinned to one external address, that address running out of ports is a problem, and the document says either drop the new connection or let it move to another external address, which is a trade-off between strictness and keeping the service up.

sections.title: Protocol Independence of Mapping and Filtering
sections.content:
REQ-1 from RFC 4787 and REQ-1 from RFC 5382 do not specify whether EIM mappings are protocol dependent or protocol independent. For example, if an outbound TCP SYN creates a mapping, it is left undefined whether outbound UDP packets can reuse such a mapping. The update is that EIM mappings should be protocol dependent. A configuration parameter may be provided to allow protocols that multiplex TCP and UDP over the same source IP address and port number to use a single mapping, and the default value of that parameter must be protocol-dependent EIM. This is consistent with the stateful NAT64 specification, which clearly specifies three binding information bases: TCP, UDP and ICMP.

REQ-8 from RFC 4787 and REQ-3 from RFC 5382 do not specify whether mappings with Endpoint-Independent Filtering (EIF) are protocol independent or protocol dependent. The update is that EIF filtering should be protocol dependent, with a configuration parameter that may make it protocol independent, and a default that must be protocol-dependent EIF. Applications that can be transported over a variety of transport protocols, or that support transport fallback schemes, will not experience connectivity failures if the NAT is configured with protocol-independent EIM and protocol-independent EIF.

The NAT mapping refresh direction may have a NAT inbound refresh behaviour of True according to REQ-6 from RFC 4787, but RFC 4787 does not clarify how this applies to EIF mappings. The issue is whether inbound packets that match an EIF mapping but do not create a new session due to a security policy should refresh the mapping timer. This document clarifies that even when the inbound refresh behaviour is set to True, such packets should not refresh the mapping, because otherwise a simple attack of a packet every two minutes could keep the mapping indefinitely. This behaviour should apply also for TCP. In the case of NAT outbound refresh behaviour, ICMP Errors or TCP RST outbound packets sent as a response to inbound packets should not refresh the mapping. Other packets that indicate the host is not interested in receiving packets may be configurable to also not refresh state, such as a STUN error response or an IKE INVALID_SYNTAX message.
sections.plainLanguage: Two decisions are now explicit. A mapping belongs to one protocol unless the operator says otherwise, and the same goes for the filtering that goes with it. And a packet that matches a mapping but is not allowed through should not keep that mapping alive, otherwise an attacker could hold it open forever with one small packet every two minutes.

sections.title: Ports, Identifiers and ICMP Mappings
sections.content:
On port parity, a NAT may disable port parity preservation for all dynamic mappings, but it should support a means to explicitly request to preserve port parity. Dynamic mappings are dynamic in the sense that they are created on demand, either implicitly or explicitly. Implicit dynamic mappings refer to mappings created as a side effect of traffic such as an outgoing TCP SYN or outgoing UDP packet, and usually have a finite lifetime that is generally not known to the client. Explicit dynamic mappings refer to mappings created as a result of, for example, explicit Port Control Protocol (PCP) MAP and PEER requests, and have a finite lifetime that is communicated to the client.

On port randomization, a NAT should follow the recommendations of Section 4 of RFC 6056. A NAPT that does not implement port preservation should obfuscate the selection of the ephemeral port of a packet when it is changed during translation. A NAPT that does implement port preservation should obfuscate the ephemeral port only if the port must be changed because it was already in use for another session. A NAPT that performs parity preservation and must change the ephemeral port during translation should obfuscate the ephemeral ports; the algorithms could easily be adapted so that parity is preserved, by forcing the lowest order bit of the resulting port number to 0 or 1 according to whether even or odd parity is desired.

A NAT should handle the Identification field of translated IPv4 packets as specified in Section 5.3.1 of RFC 6864. On ICMP, RFC 5508 specifies that ICMP Query mappings are to be maintained by a NAT but does not discuss timeout values, and this document clarifies that ICMP Query mappings may be deleted once the last session using the mapping is deleted. On hairpinning, REQ-7 from RFC 5508 specifies that a NAT enforcing Basic NAT must support traversal of hairpinned ICMP Query sessions, which implicitly means that address mappings from external address to internal address, similar to Endpoint-Independent Filters, must be maintained to allow inbound ICMP Query sessions, so that if an ICMP Query is received on an external address the NAT can then translate to an internal IP. The same requirement covers the traversal of hairpinned ICMP Error messages, which requires a NAT to maintain address mappings from external IP address to internal IP address in addition to the ICMP Query mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT may rewrite the port number it gives a connection, and if it does, it should not do so in a way an outside observer can guess. It should also rewrite the IPv4 identification field in a defined way, keep ICMP mappings only as long as a session needs them, and keep a record of external to internal addresses so a host can talk to another host behind the same NAT.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NAT behavioural considerations are discussed in RFC 4787, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508. Because some of the clarifications and updates are inspired from NAT64, the security considerations of Section 5 of RFC 6146 apply here as well.

The update in Section 3 allows for optimized NAT resource usage. In order to avoid service disruption, the NAT must not invoke this functionality unless the packets are to be sent to distinct destination addresses.

Some of the updates allow for increased security compared with the original documents. The updates in Sections 7 and 11 prevent an illegitimate node from maintaining mappings activated in the NAT while those mappings should be cleared, and port randomization complicates tracking hosts located behind a NAT. Sections 4 and 12 propose updates that increase the serviceability of a host located behind a NAT, and introduce no additional security concerns. The updates in Sections 5 and 6 allow for better NAT transparency from an application standpoint; hosts that require restricted filtering behaviour should enable specific policies, such as an Access Control List, either locally or by soliciting a dedicated security device such as a firewall.

The update in Section 8 induces security concerns specific to the protocol used to interact with the NAT; if PCP is used to explicitly request parity preservation for a given mapping, the security considerations of RFC 6887 should be taken into account. The update in Section 10 may have undesired effects on the performance of the NAT in environments in which fragmentation is massively experienced, and such an issue may be used as an attack vector against NATs.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of these changes make a NAT harder to attack, because a stray packet can no longer keep a mapping alive and the port numbers are harder to guess. One change, rewriting the identification field in IPv4 packets, costs processing when a link fragments a lot, which is worth knowing before turning it on.

items.title: Port parity
items.text: A NAT may disable parity preservation for all dynamic mappings, but should offer a way to request it.

items.title: Port randomization
items.text: When a port is changed, the choice of the new one should be obfuscated.

items.title: IP identification field
items.text: Handle the Identification field of translated IPv4 packets as specified in RFC 6864.

items.title: ICMP query mappings
items.text: May be deleted once the last session using the mapping is deleted.

items.title: Hairpinning for ICMP
items.text: Keep external to internal address mappings so hairpinned ICMP sessions work.
